# Hazards work but turn signals do not

The behavior you are describing with your 1991 Honda Accord is a classic symptom of a specific fault in the flasher relay logic or its power distribution path. When hazards function correctly while individual turn signals fail, it indicates that the primary power source and ground paths to the bulbs are intact. The issue lies entirely within the switching mechanism that differentiates left/right turns from simultaneous hazard activation.

In automotive electrical systems of this era, the flasher unit is not merely a timing circuit; it acts as a load-sensitive switch. Most OEM relays used in 1990s vehicles rely on the resistance of the bulbs to determine their internal oscillation frequency. When you engage the hazards, the relay bypasses the turn signal selection logic and completes a direct low-resistance path through both filaments simultaneously. This lower total current draw often tricks older thermal or electronic flashers into maintaining the "on" state without dropping out, or it simply forces the contact points to close regardless of the switch position. However, when you select a specific turn, the circuit expects a higher resistance load (one bulb) and attempts to oscillate at that new frequency. If the internal contacts are pitted, corroded, or if the thermal bimetallic strip is fatigued from decades of heat cycling, the relay may fail to open the circuit for the selected side while remaining closed for the hazard path, resulting in a light that stays on or refuses to flash.

To diagnose this systematically without immediately replacing parts, you must isolate the load. Disconnect the bulbs and run a multimeter across the output terminals of the flasher unit while engaging the turn signal. If you see 12V with no current draw (infinite resistance), the relay coil is energizing but the internal contacts are not closing. Conversely, if the hazard lights work, you can confirm the power feed to the unit is solid. The most common failure point in these specific Hondas is the flasher relay itself located under the dashboard or in the fuse box. These units often suffer from "stuck" contacts where the plastic housing has warped over time or the metal armature has fused to the contact points due to arcing.

Before swapping the entire relay, check for a dedicated fuse for the turn signal circuit separate from the hazard circuit. While rare on this model year, some variations of the Accord split these loads. If you find a blown fuse only in the turn signal bank and not the hazards, simply replacing it might restore function if the underlying short wasn't catastrophic enough to blow the main hazard fuse. However, given the symptoms where one side stays on then both stop, the flasher relay is almost certainly the culprit.

If you decide to upgrade the system, consider replacing the stock thermal flasher with a solid-state electronic relay or an LED-compatible version. The original Honda relays are designed for incandescent bulbs; LEDs draw significantly less current, which can cause these thermal units to fail to flash or stay permanently lit because they don't receive enough heat to trigger the oscillation mechanism. This is a frequent complaint when modernizing older cars with aftermarket lighting.

If you are comfortable working with the vehicle's wiring harness and want to ensure longevity, inspect the connector at the back of the flasher unit for corrosion or loose pins. Sometimes the issue isn't inside the relay but in the connection providing ground to the signal switch itself. A poor ground connection can cause erratic behavior where the system interprets a turn command as a hazard command due to voltage drop issues.

Replacing the flasher relay is usually a quick fix involving removing a few screws and swapping the unit, but understanding the load sensitivity of these older components helps prevent future headaches. If you are maintaining an older vehicle for reliability or preparing it for sale, addressing this electrical quirk ensures safety and prevents confusion on the road. For those who prefer not to handle automotive diagnostics, reputable auto electricians can verify the continuity of the switch and relay quickly.
